sources.title: NASA Explores Potential Commercial Servicing for Hubble Telescope

en.title: NASA Seeks Commercial Options to Extend Hubble Life
en.dek: NASA requests industry ideas to boost or service Hubble before its predicted re‑entry in 2033‑2034.
facts: NASA issued a Request for Information on Oct. 29, 2026 to learn about commercial in‑space servicing for Hubble.
The Request for Information remains open until 3 p.m. EST Nov. 30, 2026.
Hubble is expected to re‑enter Earth’s atmosphere between 2033 and 2034, so a servicing mission would need to occur by 2032.
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said extending Hubble would provide more discoveries and science.
Hubble’s altitude is decreasing because of atmospheric drag and it has no propulsion system.
body: NASA announced the Request for Information on Oct. 29, 2026. The notice invites commercial companies to propose missions that could boost Hubble to a higher orbit, service its instruments, or conduct a controlled re‑entry. The request is available online and will close on Nov. 30, 2026.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said that Hubble still has important science ahead and that extending its life would benefit the scientific community and taxpayers. He added that innovative and cost‑effective ways to extend an asset already in orbit should be explored.

Nicky Fox, associate administrator for the Science Mission Directorate, noted that commercial industry has rapidly evolved to offer new capabilities for in‑space satellite capture and servicing. She said the agency is eager to explore possibilities to boost Hubble to a higher orbit while developing the next flagship mission.
The Hubble Space Telescope was launched in 1990 and has operated for more than 30 years. It continues to make discoveries that shape our understanding of the universe.

Hubble’s altitude is slowly decreasing due to atmospheric drag, and without a propulsion system it is predicted to re‑enter between 2033 and 2034. A servicing mission would need to be completed by 2032 to keep the telescope operational.
en.context: Hubble has been a key instrument for astronomy for over 30 years, and its orbit is gradually lowering because of drag. NASA is looking for commercial partners to keep the telescope functioning longer.
